title: When seva feeds the ego
hook: serving to be seen feeds the very ego seva is meant to thin

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seva of the mind: teaching and listening. Your line was give what you know.
screen: `SEVA OF THE MIND — GIVE WHAT YOU KNOW.`

segments.voice: Saturday morning, serving food at a shelter. Good work, and a tired, happy walk home. Then a tiny voice asks: should I post about it? Just one picture. Not to brag. Just so people know. Or it's quieter than that. All the dishes at a family dinner, washed, and a small wait for someone to notice. Nobody does, and it stings. That sting is worth a look. It isn't the mark of a bad person. The Gurus wrote about it again and again, and today it gets a name.
screen: `SHOULD I POST ABOUT IT?` → `WAITING TO BE NOTICED.` → `THE STING HAS A NAME.`

segments.voice: Haumai. Hau means I. Mai means me. I, me. It's the Gurus' word for ego: the self that puts itself at the center of everything, that wants credit, that keeps count. In Sikh teaching, haumai is the main thing that stands between a person and God. Not some outside enemy. The inside one. Here's the trap this week has been building toward. Seva is meant to thin haumai: you serve, you forget yourself, the I gets a little smaller. But serve in order to be seen, and the seva itself becomes food for the ego. The more you do, the bigger it gets. Same dishes, same shoes, opposite result. That's why the Gurus keep stressing nishkam, without wanting. Now the hopeful part. Guru Angad has a line in the Guru Granth Sahib. In paraphrase: haumai is a long, deep illness, but the medicine is within it too. The place the sickness lives is where the cure can start. Noticing yourself wanting credit is already the medicine working. And Guru Nanak says in the Japji that someone who understands the divine order, the hukam, stops saying I. So the practice isn't to beat yourself up for wanting to be seen. That's just more I. Notice it, smile at it, and let it go, the way you'd smile at a child who wants you to watch them jump. Then do the next bit of service anyway.
screen: `HAU AND MAI: I, ME.` · `SEVA TO BE SEEN FEEDS THE I.` · `THE MEDICINE IS WITHIN IT TOO.` · `NOTICE IT, SMILE, LET IT GO.` · then, large: `DO THE NEXT SEVA ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last few days of seva, the unseen kindness, the shoes, the dish, the tenth, the thing you taught, and find a moment you wanted someone to know. Don't judge it; just see it clearly, like spotting a cat on a windowsill: oh, there you are. Smile at it, and let it go.
Haumai. I, me: the ego that wants credit, which seva is meant to thin, and which the Gurus say holds its own cure.
Your line: serve, then forget it. Wanting credit is human, and noticing it is the medicine. That's day one hundred two.

howItsDone: Sikh teaching names haumai, ego, as the root obstacle between a person and God, and Sikhs are taught to do seva humbly and without seeking recognition so that it thins the ego rather than feeding it.
